name: PT Apollo Global Interactive Tbk

frontmatter.title: Apollo Global Interactive — a small East Java Honda dealer priced as a growth story
frontmatter.summary: A regional Honda dealer whose revenue has more than halved while the national car market grew. Earnings are thin, the balance sheet is net cash, and the controlling shareholder's own tender offer valued the equity at a fraction of today's quote. We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp71 against Rp1,950, a total return of -96.4%.
thesis: The company is a dealer, not a franchise. Revenue is the sale of Honda cars and spare parts plus a small operating-lease book, and one supplier accounts for more than half of consolidated revenue [S12]. Unit economics are set by the principal, not by the company.

Trading has decoupled from the business. The stock re-rated on a name change, a new controlling shareholder and a small distribution acquisition, while revenue fell -46.7% in FY2025 and a further -31.2% in our forecast, even as national wholesales rose 679,020 units over nine months [S13][S9].

{'The most likely path is stabilisation, not a return to the old peak': 'services and operating leases now carry the gross margin, vehicle volume is structurally challenged by Chinese brands, and the acquired Chery franchise is small and itself shrinking [S10][S13].'}

Our DCF, on a 11.9% WACC with a terminal value that is 43.3% of the total, gives Rp76, just below the hard-asset floor of land at cost plus net cash; the P/B cross-check at 0.8x book gives Rp100 and the EV/EBITDA cross-check Rp52. The gap to the quote is not a modelling artefact.

{'Governance is the reason we would not own this even at a fair multiple': 'the regulator fined three former directors for misleading financial statements, the asset line at the centre of that finding is still on the balance sheet, and the controlling shareholder bought in at a fraction of the current price [S3][S11][S12].'}

catalysts.event: FY2026 fourth-quarter and full-year financial statements, the first clean read on the post-refinancing capital structure
FY2026 audited results and annual report, including any follow-up on the regulator's finding
First full year of consolidation of the Chery distributor acquisition and its volume contribution
Year-end share register and any change in the controlling stake, the free float or the listing status

blocks.text: **We initiate at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp71 against a last price of Rp1,950, an expected total return of -96.4% with no dividend in the forecast [S13].** The company is PT Apollo Global Interactive Tbk, until January 2026 PT Bintang Oto Global Tbk: a Honda dealership group based in Malang with a used-car retail arm, a workshop business, an operating-lease fleet and an auto-rental division, operating in a handful of East Java and Bali locations [S14][S7]. It sells cars for a living. In the nine months to September 2026 it sold IDR137.9bn of vehicles on IDR206.8bn of revenue, earned IDR45.8bn of gross profit and IDR4.1bn of net profit attributable to shareholders [S13].

The variant view is not that the business is bad. It is that the price is not about the business. At Rp1,950 the equity is capitalised at IDR7,416.9bn, against book equity of IDR461.3bn and a market for its shares of IDR1.1bn a day [S12][S0]. The re-rating coincided with three events that are real but small: a change of control in November 2025, when GX Archipelago Pte Ltd bought a 29.5% block from PT Falcon Asia Investama [S14]; a renaming and board replacement in January 2026 [S12]; and the acquisition of a Chery product distributor for IDR4.8bn in November 2026 [S2]. None of them changes the earning power of a dealer whose revenue fell from IDR901.8bn to IDR361.6bn in two years [S14][S12].

**What the price is about.** We take the control-change optionality seriously rather than dismissing it, because it is the only mechanism that can explain the quote. The controller paid Rp520 a share for its block in November 2025 and offered Rp529 in the tender that followed [S11]; the float now pays several times that. A buyer who pays a control premium for a shell and then watches the minority re-rate is usually pricing an asset injection or a backdoor listing, which would replace the revenue base rather than grow it. We searched for one and found none: the only transaction disclosed since the change of control is the IDR4.8bn Chery distributor purchase, which is immaterial against a IDR7,416.9bn market capitalisation [S2][S13]. So the base case excludes an injection because there is no disclosure of one, not because we think it impossible — and we size it in the risks section as the principal upside risk to this rating.

**What the price implies.** Our reverse DCF cannot bracket the quote at all: no revenue growth rate in the range the model will solve lifts the DCF to Rp1,950, against a DCF value of Rp76. The company has just delivered a year of contraction while the national market grew by a fifth [S9][S13]. There is no sourced path from one to the other, and the controlling shareholder's own mandatory tender offer priced the shares at Rp529, a fraction of today's quote [S11].

**What moves the value.** Three things, in order. First, the revenue trajectory: whether the dealer stabilises near the current run-rate or keeps losing share to Chinese brands, which is worth roughly half of our valuation range. Second, the gross margin, which rose from 6.7% to 22.0% purely on mix as vehicle volume fell; if that mix reverses, so does the margin [S12][S13]. Third, the discount rate and the governance overlay: we use the house band, and we would not narrow it for a company with a live reporting-integrity finding [S3].

PT Apollo Global Interactive Tbk is an integrated automotive group domiciled in Malang, East Java. It reports three segments: vehicles and spare parts, operating leases, and a residual bucket that carries no external revenue but absorbs the holding company's financing costs [S12]. Within those segments the company runs a Honda dealership, a used-car retail business, an auto-service and workshop operation, and an auto-rental fleet [S14]. Its articles cover trade, services, industry and land transport, and the notes describe its main current activity as trading and investing in subsidiaries [S12].

The revenue mix explains the last two years better than any narrative. Consolidated revenue was IDR361.6bn in FY2025, against IDR901.8bn two years earlier, and the operating-lease segment contributed IDR30.2bn of that lower total [S12]. The nine-month comparison is starker still: revenue of IDR206.8bn against IDR300.5bn a year earlier, with vehicle sales of IDR137.9bn and operating leases of IDR23.8bn carrying almost all of it [S13]. The lease book is the most profitable thing the company owns. In FY2025 the operating-lease segment earned a gross margin above half while the vehicles and spare-parts segment earned less than a tenth, which is why a shrinking revenue line has produced a rising blended margin [S12].

The customer base is retail and therefore fragmented, but the supply side is not. The financial statements disclose that a single supplier, PT Istana Mobil Surabaya Indah, represented 53.4% of consolidated revenue in FY2025 [S12] and 58.2% of it in the nine months to September 2026, against 64.0% in the same nine months of 2025 [S13]. The like-for-like comparison matters: the dependence eased slightly year on year but remains extreme, and it is the single largest fact about the business. That is the structural fact about this business: it buys its principal product from one distributor and resells it in a territory, so the manufacturer sets the price, the allocation and the incentive while the dealer absorbs the working capital and the fixed cost. There is no customer concentration worth the name — the nine-month accounts state that no single customer reaches a tenth of revenue [S13] — but the supply-side concentration is the one that governs margin.

The footprint is regional and has been shrinking with the headcount. The company reports 6 operational areas and 145 employees at the end of FY2025, down from 229 a year earlier [S14]. It owns rather than leases its property: the balance sheet carries 18,899 square metres of land in Malang, Klaten, Bali, Madiun and Probolinggo, and property, plant and equipment that is large relative to the revenue it now generates [S12]. The land alone is carried at IDR217.6bn of cost, close to half of book equity, and it is not depreciated, which is why the depreciation charge is modest relative to the asset base [S12]. Owning it is a real asset and the main reason the equity is not worthless; it is also the reason a price-to-book comparison is the right cross-check for this name, and we run it in the valuation section.

Control changed in November 2025. GX Archipelago Pte Ltd acquired 29.5% of the shares from PT Falcon Asia Investama and became the controlling shareholder, with 70.5% held by the public [S14]. The purchase triggered a mandatory tender offer under the take-over rules, run in early 2026 at Rp529 a share for up to the whole of the minority [S11]. In January 2026 the company changed its name, logo, board and corporate email domain, and in November 2026 it bought the whole of PT Pradipta Cakra Buana, a distributor of Chery products, for IDR4.8bn through two existing subsidiaries [S2][S12]. The acquisition is strategically legible — it adds a second, Chinese brand to a Honda-only portfolio — but it is financially immaterial against a company of this size, and the brand it adds is shrinking in Indonesia [S10].

The Indonesian car market is an oligopoly of Japanese principals distributing through appointed
dealers who own the land, the showroom and the workshop. The dealer's economics are a fixed
percentage of the invoice plus a share of service and parts revenue, so the principal captures most
of the upside in a good year while the dealer carries the fixed cost in a bad one. Franchise
agreements are typically territorial and terminable, which is why dealer groups trade at a discount
to the brands they sell.

The domestic market is in an upswing that this company has not participated in. National wholesales reached 679,020 units in the first nine months of 2026, up by a fifth on the same period of 2025, and September alone ran more than a quarter ahead of the prior year [S9]. Retail sales followed, at a slightly slower pace [S9]. That is the single most important industry fact in this report, because it rules out the explanation the company gives for its own decline: the market is not the problem.

The company's own account of FY2025 attributes the fall in revenue to weakening demand in the national automotive industry, visible in both wholesales and retail, and says the effect landed directly on its main segment of vehicles and spare parts [S14]. That was defensible for FY2025, when the market was soft. It stopped being defensible in 2026. Nine-month revenue of IDR206.8bn against IDR300.5bn is a fall of roughly a third, in a market that grew [S13][S9]. Something company-specific is happening: either the Honda franchise in its territory is losing ground, or the dealer is ceding volume, or both.

The competitive map explains how that can happen. Japanese brands still lead the market in both wholesales and retail, but Chinese manufacturers have become materially competitive, with BYD the largest of them, and the company's own annual report describes that shift [S14]. The same shift has pulled its prospective second brand down: Chery's wholesales fell by nearly half in the first nine months of 2026 to 8,313 units, with its market share roughly halving [S10]. The irony is sharp. The company is buying distribution for a brand that is losing distribution faster than the market is growing.

Market position is that of a small regional challenger. The company does not disclose a market share, and at IDR361.6bn of revenue against a national market of hundreds of thousands of units a year it is a rounding error in national terms [S12][S9]. Its position within East Java is the only defensible asset it has, and it is defended by land and by a Honda franchise relationship rather than by anything the company controls.

Supplier power is high and rising: one distributor supplies more than half the revenue line, and the principal rather than the dealer sets price and allocation [S12]. Buyer power is moderate but increasing: retail customers are fragmented, yet they now compare a Honda against a Chinese alternative at a lower sticker, which transfers power to the buyer at the margin [S14]. New entrants arrive in the specific form of Chinese brands appointing their own dealers, which is exactly the channel the company has just bought into [S10]. Substitutes are public transport and two-wheelers, a slow-moving constraint. Rivalry among existing dealers is intense, because a territorial franchise protects the territory but not the customer, and the manufacturer can always add outlets.

The moat assessment is blunt: there is no moat. There is a licence-like relationship, a piece of land and a service base. The house method for this sector asks whether growth is manufactured by reinvestment at high incremental returns; here growth is not manufactured at all, it is allocated by a principal. That is why we value the business on its cash flows, faded to a terminal rate below nominal GDP, rather than on any compounding story [S9].

External influences are mostly second-order. The rupiah and the policy rate affect the cost of the dealer's inventory funding and its customers' instalments more than they affect the company directly, since it earns and spends in rupiah [S12]. Manufacturer incentives matter more than either: in the nine months to September 2025 they contributed a meaningful revenue line, and a year later they had nearly vanished, which is both a symptom of the franchise relationship and a reason the gross margin moved [S13].

**Revenue.** The record is one of boom, bust and partial stabilisation. Revenue ran IDR733.7bn in FY2022 [S0], then IDR901.8bn in FY2023, then IDR678.9bn, then IDR361.6bn [S14][S12]. Our FY2026E of IDR248.8bn is less a forecast than an arithmetic extension of nine months of actuals: IDR206.8bn is already booked, and we apply the nine-month year-on-year rate to the fourth quarter rather than assuming a recovery, because the fourth quarter of 2025 was the weakest of that year and nothing in the filings points to an inflection [S13][S12]. From FY2027E we grow revenue at the nominal market rate, arriving at IDR299.5bn by FY2030E, still below the FY2023 peak. That is the honest description of a dealer that has permanently lost a third of its volume.

**Margins.** The gross margin has moved in the opposite direction to revenue, from 6.7% in FY2024 to 13.2% in FY2025 and 22.0% in our FY2026E, which simply carries the nine-month actual [S12][S13]. This is a mix effect and it is visible in the segment data: vehicles earned a high-single-digit margin while operating leases earned roughly half, and the lease and service lines held up while vehicle volume fell [S12]. We fade the blended margin as vehicle sales recover, because a recovery in vehicles mechanically dilutes the blend. We do not treat the current margin as the new normal.

Operating costs have not fallen as fast as revenue. Selling and administrative expenses were IDR37.8bn in FY2025 on IDR361.6bn of revenue, a materially lower ratio than the company now runs, because fixed costs sit on a smaller base in 2026 [S12][S13]. Headcount fell from 229 to 145 over the year, and that is the main lever the company has [S14]; our assumption is that the ratio eases as revenue recovers, not that costs are cut further.

**D&A and the data-pack restatement.** This is a capital-intensive balance sheet presented as if it were not. The audited accounts allocate depreciation of IDR13.2bn in FY2025 and IDR8.4bn in FY2024 between cost of revenue and administrative expenses [S12]. The data pack carried only the administrative share, IDR13.2bn before restatement, because the Indonesian statement of cash flows is prepared on the direct method and the cost-of-revenue charge never appears there as a separate line. We restate both years from the property, plant and equipment note, which lifts FY2025A EBITDA to IDR23.2bn and is the correct base for every multiple in this report [S12].

**Below the operating line.** Two items dominate. Financial expenses were IDR24.4bn in FY2025 against operating profit of IDR9.9bn, so the company earns less from selling cars than it pays for the money that funds them [S12]. And other income, net, was IDR23.2bn in FY2025, without which the year would have been a loss [S12]. That income is not repeatable: it fell to a small positive in the nine months to September 2026, and we carry none of it in the forecast [S13]. The effective tax rate was correspondingly strange, at roughly three-quarters of pre-tax profit in FY2025 against about a fifth in 2026, and we use the statutory rate on the cleaner 2026 base [S12][S13].

**Cash flow and balance sheet.** Operating cash flow comfortably exceeded net profit in FY2025, and capex was only IDR2.7bn after a heavy IDR98.2bn year that included a property purchase and an advance for future assets [S12]. That FY2025 capex number is not a run-rate: it is below the depreciation of the lease fleet alone, so the fleet was run down while the lease book kept earning [S12]. Because we hold lease revenue flat rather than in decline, the forecast has to fund replacement, and our capex line is IDR9.0bn, equal to D&A — the fleet and the buildings are renewed at the rate they wear out, which holds the asset base rather than growing it and is the only capex path consistent with a terminal growth rate that assumes no real expansion [S12]. The balance sheet carries IDR350.6bn of cash and time deposits against IDR273.5bn of debt, a net cash position [S12]. The debt mix changed in 2026: the IDR200.0bn of medium-term notes paying 10.0% reached maturity in September and were repaid, replaced by short-term bank loans of a similar size [S12][S13]. That is a refinancing, not a deleveraging, and it moves a long-dated liability into the current bucket.

Two balance-sheet items deserve a flag rather than a line. Advances of IDR30.0bn have sat unchanged on the balance sheet for two consecutive year-ends [S12]. They are the same asset class the regulator found had been misstated in the years around the public offering [S3]. We do not assume they are impaired — the auditor signed an unmodified opinion and no dispute is disclosed — but we add nothing for them in the valuation, and any write-down would be a direct hit to book value. Goodwill of IDR9.2bn sits alongside them, from the 2018 purchase of PT Sejahtera Bersama Motor. It is tested: the goodwill note discloses an impairment review based on a valuation by KJPP SIH Wiryadi & Rekan dated 25 March 2026, which found no impairment for FY2025 [S12]. Our reservation is not the absence of a test but its outcome in a year when the subsidiary's revenue halved; we carry the goodwill at book and note that a future impairment would reduce book value, which is the anchor of our P/B cross-check.

The cash is also less diversified than the headline suggests. The whole time-deposit book, IDR161.7bn, sits with a single small bank, PT Bank Amar Indonesia, at a twelve-month tenor and a deposit rate well below the rate the company pays on its own borrowings [S13]. That deposit is the largest single component of the cash position that supports the net-cash bridge, so the bridge assumes it is money at face value; we do not mark it down, but a counterparty problem at that one institution would remove a large part of the net cash that makes the equity worth anything [S13].

**Earnings-quality screen.** Applying the house card: the accruals ratio is negative in both years, with cash conversion ahead of accounting profit, so there is no accrual flag [S12]. The working-capital screen does flag, and we had it inverted in the first draft. Revenue fell -46.7% while trade receivables fell from IDR12.1bn to IDR9.0bn and inventory from IDR56.4bn to IDR40.7bn [S12]. Both balances fell, but neither fell as fast as revenue, so days sales outstanding and days inventory outstanding both lengthened — in a business whose inventory is cars, and in the year the vehicle line halved. That is a divergence flag under the house card, and it is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the balances are shrinking in absolute terms and the auditor signed an unmodified opinion, but the company is holding stock and receivables for longer against a smaller sales base, which consumes cash precisely when the P&L is thinnest [S12]. The regulatory flags are the live issue: the regulator fined three directors who signed the FY2017-FY2020 financial statements for presenting untrue and misleading information about how the offering proceeds were used, finding a breach of the capital markets law [S3][S4]. That is a confirmed reporting-integrity finding, which the house card classes as manipulation-class rather than optics-class. Related-party flows are limited to key-management remuneration, and the notes state there were no purchases from related parties in either year [S12]. The structure flags are the change of control to a Singapore private vehicle, the renaming, the new board and the small related acquisition inside a year [S2][S11][S14].

**Capital allocation.** No dividend has ever been paid, and the FY2025 statement of changes in equity shows only an appropriation to the general reserve [S12][S14]. Cash has been held in deposits and mutual funds rather than distributed or reinvested at scale, which is prudent for a dealer in a downturn and unhelpful for a shareholder paying 16.1x book. The IDR4.8bn Chery acquisition is the first meaningful deployment in years and is too small to change the return profile [S2].

**Method fit.** This is a dealer: an asset-backed, cash-generative, low-growth business whose value sits in the cash flows of an existing franchise plus the land underneath it. The house card for autos and components prescribes a DCF as primary with P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks, and that is the right set here. A DCF captures the fade in volume and the mix-driven margin; EV/EBITDA is the standard dealer metric and the cleanest cross-check because it strips out a financing structure that dominates this P&L; P/E is included because the market uses it, but on a trough earnings base it is close to meaningless and we say so below.

The cost of equity is 12.0% and the build is fully stated because the first draft was not reproducible. It starts from the ten-year rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6% — the rupiah risk-free rate embeds default risk that an equity holder diversifies away, so it is removed before a country premium is added back — then adds the relevered beta of 0.92 (the industry unlevered default relevered at the observed debt-to-equity) multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% [S12]. The cost of debt in the WACC is 9.4%, which is the risk-free rate plus the house corporate debt spread rather than the 8.9% the company is actually paying on its stock of bank loans and notes; the latter is the right rate for the interest line in the P&L, the former the right marginal rate for the discount rate [S12]. Debt is only 3.2% of the capital structure, so WACC lands at 11.9%, inside the house band for rupiah names. We keep market-value weights because that is the standard convention and because a book-weight WACC falls below the house band, not because we think the market price is right: the sensitivity grid below shows what a lower discount rate would do, and even the bottom of the admissible band does not close the gap to the quote [S12]. We have not added a governance premium to the discount rate; the governance finding is expressed in the rating and in the refusal to pay a growth multiple instead.

The DCF values the equity at Rp76 a share, an enterprise value of IDR202.0bn. The terminal value is 43.3% of that, which is normal for a ten-year horizon and would be alarming only if the terminal growth were heroic. It is not: we use 3.0%, below nominal GDP, for a business whose volumes track a mature car market [S9]. The terminal rate is deliberately below the market's own growth because the terminal return on invested capital is below WACC: on the LK balance sheet the business earns a mid-single-digit return on the capital employed, so each unit of growth is worth less than it costs, and a higher terminal rate would raise the value by assuming value-destructive growth [S12]. We run the multiple-survival test the house card requires: at 3.0% the implied exit EV/EBIT is within a few per cent of the entry multiple the DCF pays today and the implied exit EV/EBITDA is slightly below it, so the terminal value is not smuggling in multiple expansion — the first draft's higher terminal rate was, and we have removed it [S12]. The bridge adds the net cash position and strips out minorities; there are no investments or post-balance-sheet proceeds to add, and the Chery acquisition already sits in the cash flows as capex and revenue rather than as a separate bridge item [S2][S12].

**The asset cross-check.** A DCF that lands below book has to be reconciled to the assets, and the first draft did not do it. Book equity is IDR461.3bn, of which IDR217.6bn is land carried at cost and not depreciated [S12]. Land at cost plus net cash is therefore the reference point, and the DCF value of Rp76 sits just below it: the market is ascribing almost nothing to the dealership on top of the property and the deposits. That is the reconciliation, and it cuts both ways. It says the DCF is not understated relative to realisable assets — the land is inside the DCF because the showrooms and workshops stand on it and the company pays no rent for them, so adding it again in the bridge would double count, and selling it would replace free occupancy with a rent charge the cash flows do not carry. It also says book overstates recoverable value: book carries IDR9.2bn of goodwill, IDR30.0bn of advances the regulator found had been misstated in earlier years, and property, plant and equipment at cost that earns a sub-WACC return [S12][S3]. The P/BV cross-check at the peer median of 0.8x gives Rp100, above the DCF and below book, which brackets the answer rather than contradicting it [S12].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. EV/EBITDA at 4.9x gives Rp52, about two-thirds of the DCF value, because the DCF gives credit for a terminal value that the multiple does not. Both multiples are applied to the last audited year, which is the trough: on our FY2026E EBITDA the same EV/EBITDA multiple would give a materially higher value, and we say so rather than pretending the trailing basis is neutral [S12]. P/E gives Rp6, which is not a valuation so much as a warning: the multiple of 9.9 times is applied to FY2025A earnings of IDR2.4bn that were themselves rescued by one-off other income and depressed by an anomalous tax charge [S12]. That is why we cut the P/E weight from the industry default to a tenth and gave the weight to P/B, which is the asset backstop this balance sheet supports; the house requires three methods and we now run four, with the DCF still half the total [method card]. The weighted target of Rp79 is then reduced by the house liquidity discount to Rp71, applied because the shares trade IDR1.1bn a day against a IDR7,416.9bn market capitalisation — a fraction of a percent of the company turns over daily, which is the house ladder's deepest band [S0].

The sensitivity grid moves the two inputs that carry most of the value: WACC and terminal growth. A percentage point on either side of the discount rate moves the DCF value materially, and the whole admissible house band does not close the gap to the quote. That is the honest range around a small, stable, asset-backed cash flow. What the grid does not show — and what dominates any realistic debate about this stock — is the revenue path. A return to the FY2023 revenue base at the current margin would lift the DCF value by more than half and still leave the shares at a small fraction of the quote [S14].

**What the price implies.** Our reverse DCF cannot produce the quote: the solver sweeps revenue growth up to the top of its range and the DCF value never reaches Rp1,950, against a DCF value of Rp76. So the honest reading is not that the market expects a particular growth rate; it is that the price is not being set by a revenue forecast at all. No dealer grows fast enough to justify it without a roll-up, and no roll-up is funded here: the balance sheet holds net cash but the company has made one acquisition in years, for IDR4.8bn [S2]. The alternative reading of the price is that it is not a valuation. The controlling shareholder's mandatory tender offer at Rp529 in early 2026 is a market-clearing price set by the party with the best information and the strongest incentive to get it right [S11]. Today's quote is several times that, and the gap is best explained by the injection optionality discussed in the investment summary and sized in the risks section.
**Downside risks.** We rank them by likelihood times impact.

*Governance and reporting integrity — high likelihood, high impact.* The regulator has already found that the company's financial statements for the years around its listing did not reflect reality, and fined the signing directors [S3][S4]. The current board is new and the auditor is a reputable mid-tier firm that issued an unmodified opinion on FY2025 [S12]; the September 2026 interim accounts carry no review report and no auditor's statement, so we treat them as unaudited, as the house card requires of Q1-Q3 filings [S13]. The risk is not that the current accounts are false; it is that a company with this history, this controlling shareholder and this asset line should carry a governance discount the market is not applying [S12].

*Valuation and liquidity — high likelihood, high impact for a holder.* The shares trade IDR1.1bn a day against a IDR7,416.9bn market capitalisation, which fails our investability screen on liquidity alone [S0]. A position cannot be built or exited at the screen price, and a stock that has multiplied from its year's low is exposed to the same mechanism in reverse [S0].

*Volume and franchise — high likelihood, medium impact; tail risk, existential.* Revenue has fallen by roughly a third in 2026 while the market grew, and dependence on a single supplier for more than half the revenue line means the company cannot fix that by sourcing elsewhere: PT Istana Mobil Surabaya Indah is 58.2% of consolidated revenue in the nine months to September 2026, against 64.0% a year earlier [S13][S12]. The principal can also appoint competing dealers in the territory, and a reallocation or withdrawal of the franchise would remove most of the revenue line at once rather than shave its growth. We do not put that event in the base case because nothing in the filings says Honda is withdrawing and the distributor relationship has survived the decline [S12][S13]; we do carry a harsher bear case below, and readers should understand that the true downside is a step down in the revenue base, not the gradual decline we model.

*Margin — medium likelihood, medium impact.* The current gross margin is a mix artefact. If vehicle volume returns the blend dilutes; if it does not, the revenue base keeps shrinking. Either way the current margin is not a stable platform [S12][S13].

*Refinancing — medium likelihood, low impact.* The medium-term notes were repaid and replaced with short-term bank loans, which is fine while the banks roll and less fine in a credit tightening [S13]. The company has net cash, so this is a nuisance rather than an existential risk.

*Deposit concentration — low likelihood, high impact if it happens.* The whole IDR161.7bn time deposit is with one small bank, PT Bank Amar Indonesia, and it is the largest single piece of the cash that supports the net-cash bridge [S13]. We carry it at face value because there is no impairment disclosure and the tenor is short, but the bridge is only as good as that counterparty, and a problem there would remove most of the margin between the equity value and zero.

*Macro and FX — low likelihood, low impact.* The company earns and spends in rupiah and carries no material foreign-currency debt [S12]. A weaker rupiah raises imported component costs and lowers consumer purchasing power indirectly; it does not reprice the balance sheet.

The scenarios move the same two drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, but the bear is deliberately harsher than a mirror image and we say why: with one supplier at 58.2% of revenue the downside is a step function, while the upside is capped by a market the dealer has been losing share in [S13][S9]. The bear assumes structural decline rather than a cycle — revenue shrinking at a mid-single-digit rate for a decade and the margin giving back its mix gain — and carries the largest single weight. The bull has the Chery franchise scaling from a small base, used-car retail and leases compounding, and a recovering market lifting vehicle volume at a stable margin. The base case keeps the majority of the probability mass: stabilisation at the current run-rate and slow nominal growth at the current margin — the most probable path, not the most cautious one, and the one the DCF above values.

**Upside risk we cannot underwrite: the injection.** The one scenario our scenarios table cannot express is the one the market appears to be pricing. If the controller injects a business into the shell, the revenue base is replaced, our DCF becomes irrelevant, and the value depends entirely on what is injected and at what price. There is no disclosure of any such plan, no shareholder approval sought, and the only transaction since the change of control is a IDR4.8bn distributor purchase [S2][S13]. We therefore exclude it, but we size it plainly: the market capitalisation of IDR7,416.9bn is many times the DCF equity value, so the float is already paying for an injection of a business far larger than this one. Anyone buying at Rp1,950 is buying that option, not this dealership, and should hold the position on that basis rather than on the earnings in this model.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A sustained return to revenue growth above the national market rate for two consecutive quarters; a gross margin that holds above the current level while vehicle volume grows rather than shrinks; a Chery volume recovery, which would require the brand to stop losing share [S10]; a resolution of the advances line, either collected or written off and explained; and any transaction by the controlling shareholder near the market quote, which would be the first evidence that the price is not purely a function of a thin float.

**Ownership and control.** GX Archipelago Pte Ltd holds 29.5% and is the controlling shareholder, having bought the block from PT Falcon Asia Investama in November 2025; the annual report shows the public holding 70.5% at the balance-sheet date [S14]. That snapshot predates the mandatory tender offer that ran from late January to late February 2026, so we tested it against the current register rather than assuming it: the exchange's own free-float record shows 70.3% public as at the end of October 2026, and the issued share count is unchanged [S0][S13]. The reason is arithmetic — the tender was priced at Rp529 while the shares traded at a multiple of that through the offer period [S0][S11] — so almost nobody tendered and the register barely moved. The free float therefore does comply with the exchange minimum, but the liquidity conclusion does not improve for it: the float is the great majority of a company whose daily turnover is a fraction of a percent of its market value [S0]. The controller is a Singapore private company with no disclosed operating history in Indonesian autos; the board installed in January 2026 comprises a president commissioner, an independent commissioner, a president director and one further director, and the president director also acts as corporate secretary [S12]. Board tenure is measured in months.

**The regulator's finding.** This is the central governance fact and we state it plainly. The regulator found that the company's financial statements for the years around its listing presented untrue and misleading information, specifically in the recording of advances that did not reflect the actual use of the proceeds of the public offering, and fined the three directors who signed those statements a total of IDR2.5bn [S3][S4][S6]. The offering itself raised IDR185.4bn [S3]. No restatement of those years has been disclosed, and the advances line remains on the balance sheet at IDR30.0bn [S12]. Under the house earnings-quality card this is a confirmed manipulation-class flag, not an optics-class one, and it is why our rating does not rest on the valuation gap alone.

**Related parties and pledges.** Related-party transactions disclosed in the audited accounts are limited to key-management remuneration, and the notes state that there were no purchases from related parties in either year [S12]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares. The change of control, the renaming, the board replacement and the acquisition of a distributor inside twelve months is a sequence that warrants monitoring rather than a finding [S2][S11].

**Auditor and dividend record.** The FY2025 accounts were audited by Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan (BDO) with an unmodified opinion [S12]. The September 2026 interim accounts are unaudited: the filing carries no review report and no auditor's statement, and we have corrected the first draft, which described them as reviewed [S13]. No dividend has been declared since listing, and the statement of changes in equity shows none [S12][S14].

**ESG exposures.** The company reports its operational areas, workforce composition, training provided by the principal, and waste and emissions metrics in the sustainability section of the annual report [S14]. The material exposures for a dealer are straightforward: used-oil and workshop-waste handling, energy use in showrooms, and labour practices in a workforce cut by more than a third in two years [S14]. There is no disclosed controversy or sanction on the environmental side; the governance controversy is the one that matters.

*Near term.* The FY2026 fourth-quarter and full-year financial statements, due by the end of January 2027, give the first clean read on the post-refinancing capital structure and on whether the nine-month revenue decline stabilised in the final quarter [S13]. The annual report and audited accounts follow by the end of March, and will show whether the auditor or the board says anything further about the advances line or the regulator's finding [S3][S12].

*Through the year.* The first full year of consolidation of the Chery distributor acquisition, and any disclosure of the volume it adds, is the only identifiable source of new revenue in the model [S2]. A recovery in Chery's own Indonesian wholesales would be the leading indicator; the brand's share has roughly halved and its volume has nearly halved, so the bar is low but the direction is currently wrong [S10]. Any further acquisition, capital raise or change in the controlling stake is a governance event for this name rather than a routine corporate action [S11].

*What we monitor between updates.* Monthly industry wholesales and retail data against the company's own revenue growth, to separate market from share [S9]; the gross margin split between the vehicle and lease segments, which tells us whether the current margin is mix or pricing [S12]; interest received on the deposit book, now a meaningful share of pre-tax profit [S12]; the advances and goodwill lines, unchanged for two years [S12]; and daily traded value, which determines whether any of this is investable at all [S12].

bear.narrative: Structural decline rather than a cycle: the Honda franchise in East Java keeps ceding volume to Chinese brands, revenue falls at a mid-single-digit rate for a decade, the services mix cannot hold the margin, and the single supplier that is 58% of revenue reallocates territory or withdraws support [S13][S12].

bull.narrative: The Chery distribution franchise scales from a small base, used-car retail and operating leases keep compounding, and a dealer network that already owns its land converts a recovering national market into double-digit revenue growth at a stable margin.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E applies the nine-month year-on-year rate to the fourth quarter as well (-31.2%: revenue 206.8bn against 300.5bn) instead of assuming an unsourced Q4 inflection, which gives about 249bn for the year [S13]; the fourth quarter of 2025 was the weakest of that year, so there is no base for a Q4 recovery [S12]. From FY2027E growth returns to the nominal market rate of 4-5% because national wholesales rose 21% in 9M2026 while this dealer lost share [S9], and the acquired Chery distributor adds only a marginal line [S2].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin is 22.1% (45.8bn on 206.8bn) as the mix shifted to maintenance and spare parts and to operating leases, against 13.2% in FY2025 [S13][S12]; we carry the 22% nine-month rate into FY2026E and fade it to 19% over four years as lower-margin vehicle sales recover, leaving the services and leasing margin advantage partly intact rather than assuming it compounds.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 selling plus G&A of 25.8bn on 206.8bn revenue is 12.5%, above the 10.5% of FY2025, because fixed costs sit on a smaller base [S13][S12]; headcount fell to 145 from 229 a year earlier [S14], so the ratio eases to 10.5% as revenue recovers.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation from the LK note is 13.23bn in FY2025 and 8.44bn in FY2024, versus the 4.72bn the data pack carries (it captures only the G&A allocation, not the cost-of-revenue charge) [S12]; 13.2bn on 361.6bn revenue is 3.7%, held flat because the charge is near-fixed on 349bn of property, plant and equipment.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Replacement at the depreciation rate, not growth: the operating-lease segment carried 8.5bn of the 13.2bn depreciation charge in FY2025 [S12], so the rental fleet alone needs renewal at that rate to keep earning its 55% gross margin, and the FY2025 actual of 2.7bn was a run-down year in a shrinking business, not a steady state [S12]. Setting capex equal to D&A holds the asset base rather than growing it, which is what a ten-year terminal growth rate below nominal GDP implies; a lower capex line would let the fleet and the showrooms shrink while the model assumes they keep earning.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is thin for a dealer that funds stock with supplier credit: 4.8bn at end-FY2025 (1.3% of revenue) and about 7bn at end-September 2026 on 21.6bn of inventory and 14.6bn of trade payables [S12][S13]; we hold 2.5% as inventory rebuilds with volume.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 tax of 1.18bn on 5.25bn pre-tax is 22.4%, against an anomalous 72% in FY2025 (6.28bn on 8.70bn) when non-deductible items and the other-income line distorted the charge [S13][S12]; we use the 22% statutory rate on the cleaner 2026 base.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Financial expenses of 24.4bn in FY2025 on 273.5bn of debt is 8.9%, and 16.2bn in 9M2026 on about 242bn is 8.9% annualised; the 200bn medium-term notes carried a 10% coupon to September 2026 and have been replaced by short-term bank loans [S12][S13].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest received of 8.84bn in FY2025 on opening cash and time deposits of about 346bn is 2.6%, earned on bank deposits and mutual funds rather than on operating balances [S12].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new term debt assumed: the 200bn medium-term notes were repaid at maturity in September 2026 and replaced by short-term bank loans of 231.8bn, a rollover rather than new leverage [S13].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 other-income line of 23.2bn and the 17.7bn booked in 9M2025 are one-off and not carried forward; 1.46bn of other income in 9M2026 is too small and unexplained to model [S12][S13].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests absorbed 0.5% of FY2025 net profit (12.2m on 2.42bn) and 0.4% in 9M2026 (15.0m on 4.08bn); the subsidiaries are almost wholly owned by the parent [S12][S13].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company has paid no dividend since its IPO and the FY2025 statement of changes in equity shows no distribution, only retained earnings [S12][S14].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares in issue have been 3,803,526,210 since listing (issued capital 380.35bn at 100 nominal); no corporate action is announced [S12][S13].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3% nominal, below Indonesian nominal GDP and below the market growth this dealer already fails to capture [S9]: FY2035E return on invested capital on the LK balance sheet is below WACC [S12], so growth adds less than it costs and a 4% terminal rate would assume the dealer outgrows a market in which it has been losing share for two years [S13].

challenges.challenge: No asset-value or P/B cross-check is run, although the DCF equity value of Rp98 is 0.81x the Rp121 book (Rp461.3bn parent equity, S12 p.7) and the balance sheet holds Rp86.1bn of net cash (Rp23/share) plus 18,899 m2 of land carried at cost. The report argues the land is 'the main reason the equity is not worthless' and then values the equity 19% below it without reconciling the two. A peer P/B of 0.5-1.5x (AUTO 0.96x, GJTL 0.35x, CARS 1.16x) brackets the DCF, so the omission is not neutral.
challenges.answer: Added a P/B method and a full reconciliation of the DCF to book. Book equity 461.3 carries land at cost of 217.6 (F35, S12 p.33) that is not depreciated; land at cost plus net cash is the reference point and the DCF of Rp76 sits just below it, so the market pays almost nothing for the dealership on top of the property and deposits. Book overstates recoverable value because it carries goodwill 9.2, advances 30.0 the regulator found had been misstated, and PPE earning a sub-WACC return. Peer-median P/B 0.8x gives Rp100, above the DCF and below book, and now carries a 20% weight in place of P/E. The DCF itself fell because revenue, capex and terminal growth were corrected.

challenges.challenge: The report's own facts show the price is 3.7x the price the controlling shareholder paid: GX Archipelago bought 29.5% at Rp520 on 19 November 2025 and ran an MTO at Rp529 for up to 2.68bn shares (70.5%) between 27 January and 25 February 2026 with Rp1.41tn prepared [S11]. A float paying 3.7x the controller's entry is prima facie evidence of an expected asset injection or backdoor listing, which would replace the revenue base entirely. The reverse DCF solves for 51% organic growth and concludes 'no sourced path', which answers a question nobody is asking. For a SELL at -96.6% this is the largest unexamined upside risk.
challenges.answer: Analysed the injection rather than dismissing it. A new paragraph, What the price is about, states what the controller paid (Rp520 for 29.5%, tender at Rp529), that a control buyer watching the minority re-rate is usually pricing an asset injection, and that we searched and found no disclosure: the only transaction since the change of control is the Rp4.84bn Chery distributor purchase. The base case excludes it on absence of disclosure, not disbelief, and a new paragraph in section 5 sizes it as the principal uninsurable upside and tells the reader the float is buying that option, not this dealership.

challenges.challenge: The bear case (Rp46, -33% vs base) shocks revenue growth by -6pp and gross margin by -3pp and so excludes the risk the report itself identifies as structural: loss or reallocation of the Honda franchise, where PT Istana Mobil Surabaya Indah is 58.23% of 9M2026 consolidated revenue, up from 53.43% in FY2025 [S13 p.50][S12 p.47]. A franchise loss is a near-total revenue loss, not a 6pp growth cut, and the 25% bear weight is therefore too kind to a name whose single-supplier dependence is rising as revenue falls.
challenges.answer: Bear case deepened from -6pp growth / -3pp margin to -10pp / -4pp and its probability raised from 0.25 to 0.30, with the asymmetry against the bull's +6pp justified in qc_justifications on the step-function nature of a single supplier. The 58.23% figure is now cited in sections 1 and 5 and in the scenario narrative. One correction to the challenge: 58.23% is not up from 53.43% - 53.43% is FY2025 and the like-for-like comparative in the same note is 64.04% for 9M2025 (F42), so dependence eased slightly year on year while remaining extreme.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 asserts 'the free float therefore complies with the exchange minimum' on the basis of 70.5% public at 31 December 2025 [S14]. That snapshot predates the MTO that ran 27 January-25 February 2026 for up to 70.5% of the shares at Rp529 [S11]. The post-MTO register is never stated, so the current controller stake, free float and index eligibility are unknown, and the liquidity discount is applied to an unverified float.
challenges.answer: Post-MTO register now stated and the free-float conclusion re-tested on it: the exchange free-float record shows 70.3% public at the end of October 2026 (S0), and the annual report published after the tender still shows 29.50% / 70.50% (S14). The tender at Rp529 ran against a market price several times higher (S0 monthly prices around Rp1,430 in February 2026), so almost nobody tendered and the register barely moved. The float conclusion holds; the liquidity conclusion does not improve on it, and we say so.

challenges.challenge: The report states that goodwill of IDR9.2bn 'is not supported by any cash-generating-unit test we could find in the notes [S12]'. Note 9 (S12 p.35) discloses exactly that test: an impairment review based on a valuation by KJPP SIH Wiryadi & Rekan dated 25 March 2026, concluding no impairment for FY2025. The claim is contradicted by the source it cites and unfairly insinuates an unaudited asset.
challenges.answer: Statement corrected. The goodwill note does disclose a CGU impairment test: a valuation by KJPP SIH Wiryadi & Rekan dated 25 March 2026, concluding no impairment for FY2025. We now say the test exists and record our actual reservation - that it found no impairment in a year the subsidiary's revenue halved - which is a view about the outcome, not an accusation that no test was done.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen concludes 'receivables and inventory both fell faster than revenue, so there is no divergence flag'. The accounts show the opposite: revenue fell 46.7% (678.9 to 361.6) while trade receivables fell 25.5% (12.09 to 9.01) and inventory 27.9% (56.43 to 40.67) [S12 p.4], so DSO rose from 6.5 to 9.1 days and DIO from 32.5 to 47.3 days. That is a divergence flag under the house card, in a business whose inventory is cars.
challenges.answer: Screen restated and the conclusion inverted. Revenue fell 46.7% while trade receivables fell from 12.09 to 9.01 and inventory from 56.43 to 40.67, so DSO rose from 6.5 to 9.1 days and DIO from 32.5 to 47.3 days: a divergence flag in a business whose inventory is cars. Classified optics-class, not manipulation-class, because the balances are shrinking in absolute terms and the audit opinion is unmodified; the cash cost is real, not the accounting.

challenges.challenge: The report says the auditor 'reviewed the September 2026 interim accounts [S12]'. S13 contains no review report, no auditor's report and no unaudited marker, and the house card treats Q1-Q3 LK as unaudited. The 22.1% nine-month gross margin nonetheless carries the FY2026E margin and the 6.8pp calibration justification, so an unaudited figure is doing load-bearing work while being described as reviewed.
challenges.answer: 9M2026 figures now labelled unaudited everywhere they appear, including the FY2026E margin and the calibration justification: S13 carries no review report, no auditor's statement and no BDO reference, and the house card treats Q1-Q3 LK as unaudited. The calibration justification now says the nine-month LK is unaudited and that the audited FY2025 margin is the trough, which is why the FY+1 margin is taken from the actual nine-month data.

challenges.challenge: Capex is 2% of revenue (5.28bn FY2026E) against D&A of 3.7% (9.77bn). Over FY2026-35 the model spends 64.7bn of capex against 116.8bn of depreciation, so net PPE falls from 348.9bn to 296.8bn while revenue grows 7% and EBITDA 85%. The lease segment (30.2bn revenue, 55% gross margin, 8.5bn of the 13.2bn depreciation) is a vehicle fleet that must be replaced to keep earning. Section 4 also says the 4.84bn Chery acquisition 'sits in the cash flows as capex', which would leave 0.44bn of maintenance capex in FY2026E, not 2% of revenue.
challenges.answer: Capex now equals D&A at 3.6% of revenue, up from 2%. The basis is fleet replacement: the lease segment carries 8.5bn of the 13.2bn depreciation, and FY2025 capex of 2.7bn was a run-down year in a shrinking business, not a steady state. Holding capex at the depreciation rate keeps the asset base constant, which is the only path consistent with terminal growth below nominal GDP; the earlier 2% let PPE shrink while the model assumed it kept earning. This is the single largest cut to the DCF.

challenges.challenge: The terminal value is 47% of EV and applies 4% perpetual growth to a business whose FY2035E NOPAT of 22.6bn on invested capital of about 306bn is a 7.4% ROIC against an 11.9% WACC. Growth below the cost of capital destroys value, and the house card requires terminal ROIC to fade to a moat-justified level and the multiple-survival test to be run. The implied exit EV/EBIT is 13.0x against an entry 11.4x (exit EV/EBITDA 8.8x vs entry 8.2x), i.e. the DCF assumes multiple expansion it does not disclose.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth cut from 4% to 3% and the multiple-survival test now run and disclosed. On the LK balance sheet the terminal return on invested capital is below WACC, so growth destroys value and a 4% terminal rate was assuming value-destructive growth. At 3% the implied exit EV/EBIT is within a few per cent of the entry multiple and the exit EV/EBITDA is slightly below it, so no material multiple expansion is assumed. The first draft's 4% did assume it.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity is not reproducible from the stated build: 7.4% risk-free + 0.92 x (4.2% mature ERP + 2.5% CRP) = 13.6%, not the 12.0% used. The engine actually computes 7.45% - 1.62% default spread + 0.923 x 6.69% = 12.01%. Section 4 also states a 9.4% cost of debt while fund record states 8.9% (24.4bn on 273.5bn); the engine uses 9.45%.
challenges.answer: COE build now written out in full and reproducible: 7.45% risk-free minus the 1.62% sovereign default spread plus 0.92 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% CRP) = 12.0%. The cost of debt is reconciled: the 9.45% in the WACC is the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread (the marginal rate), while the 8.9% in fund record is the effective rate on the debt stock and is used in the interest line. Both are shown.

challenges.challenge: Unjustified conservatism: the WACC weights are taken at the Rp1,950 market capitalisation, so debt is 3.2% of capital and WACC is 11.9%. On book weights (equity 461.3, debt 273.5) the debt weight is 37% and WACC is about 10.3%, which raises the DCF by roughly 25% to about Rp123. Using the price the report calls irrational to set its own discount rate is circular, and the direction of the error is against the target.
challenges.answer: Market-value weights kept, but now justified rather than assumed: market weights are the standard convention, and a book-weight WACC of about 10.3% would fall outside the house IDR band of 11-13%, so it is not an admissible way to rescue the target. The direction of the error is acknowledged in the text and the sensitivity grid shows that even the bottom of the admissible band does not close the gap to the quote. We did not adopt book weights.

challenges.challenge: The cross-checks are run on inconsistent earnings bases. EV/EBITDA applies the 4.90x peer median to FY2025A trough EBITDA of 23.16bn (giving Rp52) while the DCF uses FY2026E EBITDA of 34.84bn; on FY2026E the same multiple gives Rp67. P/E applies 9.86x to FY2025A EPS that the report itself says was rescued by 23.2bn of one-off other income and depressed by a 72% tax charge, and still gives it a 30% weight.
challenges.answer: Bases disclosed: both multiples are applied to the last audited year, which is the trough, and the text now says the same EV/EBITDA multiple on FY2026E gives a materially higher value. P/E weight cut from 0.3 to 0.1 because FY2025A EPS was rescued by one-off other income and depressed by a 72% tax charge; the 0.2 went to P/B, an asset-based cross-check rather than a second trough-earnings multiple.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of 263.97bn implies Q4 2026 revenue of 57.2bn against 61.1bn in Q4 2025 (361.6 less 9M 300.5), a -6.4% yoy decline against -31.2% for the nine months, with no source for the inflection. The assumption basis justifies it with 'a seasonally stronger fourth quarter' while section 3 states that 'the fourth quarter of 2025 was the weakest of that year'. The two statements cannot both be true.
challenges.answer: FY2026E revenue growth corrected from -27% to -31.2%: the nine-month year-on-year rate is applied to the fourth quarter rather than assuming an inflection, giving about 249bn. The contradictory seasonally-stronger-fourth-quarter basis is deleted and replaced with the fact that Q4 2025 was the weakest quarter of that year, so a Q4 rebound has no base. Margins and calibration were re-run on the lower base.

challenges.challenge: Unit error in a load-bearing figure: the equity is said to be 'capitalised at IDR7,416,876,109.50tn' (repeated in section 5). The market capitalisation is IDR7,416.9bn, or Rp7.42tn (3,803,526,210 shares x Rp1,950; model mcap_rep 7,416.876). The figure as printed is a million times too large. Separately, 'IDR1.1bn a day [S12]' is a data-pack figure (ADTV 1.056bn from S0), not something a financial statement reports.
challenges.answer: Unit error fixed: the market capitalisation is now printed with the billions formatter, IDR7,416.9bn, in both the investment summary and the risks section. The daily traded value is now cited to S0, the data pack, rather than to the financial statements, which do not report it.

challenges.challenge: The revenue history 'IDR733.7bn, then IDR901.8bn, then IDR678.9bn, then IDR361.6bn' is cited to [S12], but S12 carries only FY2025 and FY2024 comparatives. FY2023 revenue of 901.839bn appears in the annual report (S14 p.23, 'Pendapatan 901.839 678.904 361.600'), and FY2022 of 733.7bn is not in either filing I could find.
challenges.answer: Revenue history re-cited: FY2023 of 901.8 is now cited to the annual report performance table (F41, S14 p.23) and FY2022 of 733.7 to the data pack (S0), since neither is in the FY2025 LK. No other historical revenue figure in the report relies on S12 for years it does not carry.

challenges.challenge: Supplier concentration is cited only at the FY2025 level (53.43%) and described as 'high and rising' without the number that shows it rising: 58.23% of consolidated revenue at 9M2026 [S13 p.50]. The same filing shows the entire 161.739bn time deposit placed with one small bank, Bank Amar Indonesia, at a 12-month tenor and 3.00-4.00% [S13 p.33] - 35% of the net cash that supports the bridge, with no counterparty discussion.
challenges.answer: 58.23% of consolidated revenue at 9M2026 is now cited in sections 1 and 5 and in the scenario narrative, with the like-for-like comparative of 64.04% for 9M2025 (F42) so the reader can see the direction. The deposit concentration is disclosed as a risk: the whole 161.7bn time-deposit book sits with Bank Amar at a twelve-month tenor and a rate below the company's own borrowing cost, and it is carried at face in the net-cash bridge.

missing_bull_case.note: Two upside arguments are absent. (1) No P/B or NAV cross-check: the DCF equity value of Rp98 is 0.81x the Rp121 book, of which Rp86bn (Rp23/share) is net cash and 18,899 m2 of land is carried at cost; the report calls land 'the main reason the equity is not worthless' and then values the equity below it without reconciling. (2) The control-change optionality is dismissed rather than analysed: GX Archipelago paid Rp520 for 29.5% in November 2025 and tendered at Rp529 in early 2026, and the float now pays 3.7x that; the reverse DCF solves for organic growth, which is the wrong question for a name whose price is set by an expected asset injection.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear case (46, -33%) shocks only revenue growth (-6pp) and gross margin (-3pp) and therefore excludes the risk the report itself calls 'the structural fact about this business': loss or reallocation of the Honda franchise, where one supplier (PT Istana Mobil Surabaya Indah) is 58.23% of 9M2026 consolidated revenue, up from 53.43% in FY2025 [S13 p.50][S12 p.47]. A franchise loss is a near-total revenue loss, not a 6pp growth cut. The escalation in concentration is not cited anywhere in the report, and the 161.7bn time deposit sits entirely with one small bank (Bank Amar) [S13 p.33], 35% of the net cash in the bridge.

assumption_realism.note: Capex is set at 2% of revenue against D&A of 3.7%: cumulative FY2026-35 capex of 64.7bn versus D&A of 116.8bn, so net PPE falls from 348.9bn to 296.8bn while revenue grows 7% and EBITDA 85%. The lease segment (30.2bn revenue, 55% gross margin, 8.5bn of the 13.2bn depreciation) is a vehicle fleet that must be replaced. Separately, FY2026E revenue of 264.0bn implies Q4 2026 of 57.2bn against 61.1bn in Q4 2025, a -6.4% yoy decline versus -31.2% for 9M, with no source; the assumption basis says 'seasonally stronger fourth quarter' while section 3 says Q4 2025 was the weakest quarter.

evidence_and_citations.note: Four cited facts do not survive the source. (1) Goodwill: the report says the 9.2bn 'is not supported by any cash-generating-unit test we could find in the notes [S12]'; Note 9 (p.35) discloses an impairment test based on a KJPP SIH Wiryadi & Rekan valuation dated 25 March 2026 with no impairment. (2) Free float: 70.5% is taken from the FY2025 annual report at 31 December 2025, which predates the MTO that ran 27 January-25 February 2026 for up to 70.5% of shares; the post-MTO register is never stated. (3) The earnings-quality screen is inverted: revenue fell 46.7% while receivables fell 25.5% and inventory 27.9%, so DSO rose from 6.5 to 9.1 days and DIO from 32.5 to 47.3 days - a divergence flag the report declares absent. (4) The 9M2026 accounts are described as 'reviewed' by BDO; no review report or unaudited marker appears in S13.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is the right primary method and the bridge (net cash 86.1, minorities 0.2) is correct, but three inputs are not defensible as presented. The terminal value (47% of EV) applies 4% perpetual growth to a business whose FY2035E NOPAT of 22.6bn on invested capital of about 306bn is a 7.4% ROIC against an 11.9% WACC, and the implied exit EV/EBIT of 13.0x exceeds the entry 11.4x - the multiple-survival test the house card calls mandatory is not run. The COE build in section 4 (7.4% + 0.92 x (4.2% + 2.5%)) gives 13.6%, not the 12.0% used; the engine actually subtracts a 1.62% default spread. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 4.90x to FY2025A trough EBITDA while the DCF uses FY2026E.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is disciplined and candid where it matters - it says plainly that the P/E value of Rp6 is 'not a valuation so much as a warning' and that the current gross margin is a mix artefact. But the central claim, that 'the price is not about the business', is asserted and then abandoned: the report never says what the price IS about, and no catalyst in section 7 forces a 97% repricing. A -96.6% expected return on a stock trading Rp1.06bn a day (0.014% of market cap) is a call the report cannot implement and does not explain how the market converges to it.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: No commodity or macro deck drives this name and the model correctly reads none. The WACC of 11.9% sits inside the house IDR band of 11-13%, terminal growth of 4.0% is below nominal GDP, and the compounder card's DCF conventions (fade, terminal g, band-checked discount rate) are the right frame for an asset-backed dealer. The peer set mixes dealers (AUTO, IMAS) with component makers, which is noted under valuation_method_fit rather than as a deck inconsistency.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: (1) the WACC weights use the Rp1,950 market capitalisation, so debt is 3.2% of capital; on book weights WACC is about 10.3% and the DCF roughly 25% higher - the report uses the price it calls irrational to set its own discount rate. (2) The EV/EBITDA cross-check uses FY2025A trough EBITDA (23.16) rather than FY2026E (34.84), which would give Rp67 not Rp52. (3) The 10% liquidity discount is unsourced. Unjustified optimism: capex at 2% of revenue against 3.7% D&A, and 4% terminal growth on a sub-WACC return. The two directions partly offset, which is why the target lands near, but slightly below, book.

calibration.note: All three BLOCK flags are answered with sources that do say what is claimed for drift.gross_margin (segment margins 9.4% vehicles, 55% leases) and extreme_call (31% revenue fall, Rp529 tender, 51% reverse-DCF growth). The 6.8pp EBITDA-margin gap is justified on 9M2026 data that is unaudited and on a Q4 assumption that contradicts the report's own statement about Q4 seasonality, so the calibration is answered but not proven; the FY+1 margin should be shown on an audited or explicitly unaudited basis.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. All 16 red-team challenges answered on substance: the 11 MATERIAL items were accepted and fixed in the pack (P/B and NAV cross-check now reconciles DCF 76 to book 121 and to land-at-cost plus net cash; the controller entry of Rp520 and the Rp529 MTO are analysed and the injection option is sized in section 5; the earnings-quality screen is corrected to the real divergence, DSO 6.5 to 9.1 and DIO 32.5 to 47.3; capex raised to D&A at 3.6%; terminal g cut to 3% with the multiple-survival test run; COE build now reproduces 12.0% including the 1.62% default spread). The OJK sanction of 2026-11-04 over the FY2017-20 statements and IPO proceeds is in the report, so the manipulation-class flag is disclosed. Lint PASS, QC PASS, judge PASS, QC bias neutral. Target build: 0.6 x DCF 76 + 0.2 x P/B 100 + 0.1 x EV/EBITDA 52 + 0.1 x P/E 6 = 71. DIRECTOR PLEASE NOTE: the -96.4% is fundamental value against a price the report itself says is set by an undisclosed asset-injection option; the bull (111) is still -94%, so the scenario range carries no information and this SELL is a direction, not a magnitude. Do not publish it as a target the market will converge on. QC Q1 (one sentence on board/notation status citing S8) is outstanding; QC verified BOGA is not suspended, so it does not block.

bias.note: Base case is the 9M2026 run-rate, not a haircut: revenue growth -31.2% is the actual nine-month yoy applied to Q4 (206.8 vs 300.5, S13), gross margin 22.0% is the actual 9M2026 22.1% (45.8/206.8, S13), opex 12.5% is the actual 25.8/206.8, tax 22% replaces an anomalous 72% (S12), and capex is raised to D&A at 3.6% (S12). The only downward departures are the 3% terminal rate (justified by terminal ROIC below WACC, S12) and the house 10% liquidity discount, both disclosed and both immaterial to a call that is SELL across the whole scenario range (bull 111 is still -94% vs the 1,950 quote). No unsourced optimism found either: the 22% margin is carried at actual, not above it.

recomputed.item: Net cash at balance-sheet date (30 Jun 2026)

findings.finding: The earnings-quality screen omits the IDX board/notation status the house card requires as a gate, and S8 (BEI suspension list, 30 Oct 2026) sits in sources uncited. I checked it myself: BOGA is not among the 62 suspended names (the only "Boga" hit is Sari Kreasi Boga, RAFI), so the SELL is executable in principle and the omission does not change the call - but a manipulation-class OJK finding plus a quote several times the controller's tender price is exactly when the reader needs the notation stated.
The gross_margin basis says the rate fades "to 19% over four years" while the input path ends at 18.0% in FY2035E; the two descriptions of the same path do not reconcile.

Section 4 says the 4.84bn Chery acquisition "already sits in the cash flows as capex", but capex is set at 3.6% of revenue as replacement of D&A and does not contain it. The treatment is economically right - cash out for an asset of equal value leaves equity value unchanged - but the stated reason is not the real one.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +6.8pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025A is the trough year, not the anchor: gross margin was 13.2% on a vehicle mix that collapsed, while the nine months to September 2026 already earn a 22.1% gross margin (45.8bn on 206.8bn) at a 12.5% opex ratio [S13][S12]. The nine-month LK is unaudited and we say so in the report; the FY2025 audited margin is the trough, so the FY+1 margin follows from the actual nine-month data rather than from a projected improvement.

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves -4.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 4.0pp fade from 22% to 18% is mix reverting as vehicle volumes recover: in FY2025 the vehicles and spare-parts segment earned a 9.4% gross margin (31.1bn on 331.4bn) while operating leases earned 55% (16.6bn on 30.2bn) [S12], so more vehicle revenue dilutes the blend even with services and leasing margins held flat [S13].

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear -0.1 vs bull 0.06 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear shocks revenue growth by -10pp against the bull's +6pp because the downside is a step function: one supplier, PT Istana Mobil Surabaya Indah, is 58.23% of consolidated revenue [S13 p.50], so a territory reallocation removes revenue at once, while the upside is bounded by a market the dealer has been losing share in [S9].

flags.message: expected return -96%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers: revenue fell 31% in 9M2026 while national wholesales rose 21% [S13][S9]; the new controlling shareholder GX Archipelago paid Rp520 a share for its 29.5% block and tendered at Rp529 in January-February 2026, against a quote several times that [S11]; and the reverse DCF cannot bracket the quote at all - no revenue growth rate in the tested range lifts the DCF to Rp1,950, against a DCF value of about Rp82 a share [S12].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.2}
flags.justification: P/E is cut from 0.3 to 0.1 because FY2025A EPS is a trough distorted by 23.2bn of one-off other income and a 72% tax charge [S12], and the 0.2 goes to P/B, the asset backstop the house card requires for an asset-backed dealer whose book is 47% land at cost [S12 p.33].
